one_liner: Rust (Tokio/Hyper) reverse proxy and gateway; HAProxy and Envoy wins come from an unequal harness; nginx beats it.
what_it_does: Spire (renamed from Silverwind) is a standalone reverse proxy and gateway binary configured by one YAML file (spire -f config.yaml), with a REST admin API on admin_port for config, Prometheus metrics and certificate upload. It proxies HTTP/1.1, HTTPS, HTTP/2, gRPC and raw TCP/TLS, routes by path, host, header, weight, round-robin or random, and has middleware for API-key and Basic auth, IP allow/deny lists, CORS, token-bucket rate limiting, circuit breaking, health checks and ACME certificates. It is not a library and has no nginx or HAProxy config compatibility.
how_it_is_fast: Nothing beyond a standard async Rust stack: a Tokio multi-threaded work-stealing runtime with one task per accepted connection, a Hyper 1.x HTTP/1.1 server, and the hyper-util legacy pooled client for upstream keep-alive (default pool settings, not overridden in http_client.rs). mimalloc is the global allocator and rustls with ring does TLS. There is no io_uring, per-core SO_REUSEPORT sharding or zero-copy splice, and the release profile is not tuned (lto = false, codegen-units = 16, panic = unwind).
when_to_use: You want one Rust binary that bundles gateway features (rate limiting, circuit breaker, API-key/Basic auth, IP lists, CORS, health checks, ACME, hot reload, Prometheus) behind a single YAML file.
Moderate HTTP/1.1 reverse-proxy load: around 100k req/s on 4 cores of a desktop CPU in the author's Docker run is enough headroom for your service.
You prefer a memory-safe stack with rustls instead of OpenSSL for TLS termination.
You want an HTTP-to-gRPC route that calls a gRPC backend and returns JSON (prost-reflect path in proxy/http1/http_proxy.rs).
when_not_to_use: Raw proxy throughput or tail latency is the goal: tuned nginx 1.23.3 beats it in its own table (148,677 vs 114,512 req/s; p99 4.9 vs 11.8 ms), and in the 2023 run where every proxy had the same load generator it reached 0.81x HAProxy.
Memory-constrained hosts: issue #59 reports it used the most memory of the proxies tested, and that third-party run lists 280 MB for Silverwind vs 85 MB HAProxy, 70 MB Envoy and 40 MB nginx.
High-cardinality URL spaces: request metrics are labelled with the raw path and query string, so every distinct URL creates new Prometheus series.

You need a mature, widely deployed proxy: pre-1.0 (0.0.28), one maintainer, 74 crates.io downloads, and the config schema changed between releases (the benchmark's app_config.yaml uses the old services/listen_port schema).
You need response compression (issue #56 'Add encoding for the response' is open), HTTP/3 or caching (none documented).

integration.form: crate (binary crate spire-proxy on crates.io), prebuilt binaries and a Docker image
integration.dependencies: Tokio 1.49, Hyper 1.8 and hyper-util, rustls 0.23 (ring), mimalloc, axum, tonic, prost-reflect, prometheus, tracing and about 60 other crates pinned with = in rust-proxy/Cargo.toml
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.85+ in practice (Cargo.toml uses edition 2024); the README's 'Rust 1.70+' badge is out of date
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows per README; release binaries for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu and aarch64-apple-darwin; mimalloc is skipped on MSVC targets
integration.thread_safety: not applicable (standalone multi-threaded process); not documented
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it replaces nginx, HAProxy or Envoy as a reverse proxy, but with its own YAML config, admin API and feature set

gotchas: Harness flaw beyond the verifier's 12-vs-4-CPU finding: docker 'cpus: 4.0' sets a CFS quota, not a CPU mask. HAProxy 2.7 defaults nbthread to the CPUs in its affinity mask, and Envoy 1.22.8 defaults --concurrency to the number of hardware threads, so both probably ran about 20 threads (i5-13600K) inside a 4-CPU quota. nginx was pinned to 4 workers, and Tokio sizes its pool from std::thread::available_parallelism, which honours cgroup quotas. CFS throttling would fit the 40-51 ms tail clusters in the HAProxy and Envoy histograms (inferred, not measured).

The benchmark compose sets JEMALLOC_SYS_WITH_MALLOC_CONF at run time, but that is a build-time jemalloc-sys option, and Spire's global allocator is mimalloc (Cargo.toml at benchmark commit 0cac057 and now), so the variable does nothing; the record's 'jemalloc' note is wrong.

Every proxied request writes an info-level access-log line and updates two Prometheus metrics labelled by raw path; each HTTPS accept clones the rustls ServerConfig under a std RwLock and logs the whole config at info level.

Upstream connection errors and timeouts come back as HTTP 500 with a JSON body ('Request time out, the uri is ...'), not 502/504, and failures in the outer adapter return 404 with JSON. The Host header is rewritten to the upstream host.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Spire over routez or rproxy (whose catalogued wins over nginx and HAProxy come from tighter harnesses, rproxy's median of 3 runs on pinned cores) only when you want the bundled gateway features more than raw proxy speed. To replace Envoy specifically, Orion Proxy and linkerd2-proxy carry Envoy comparisons.
verified_claims_summary: The author ran hey -n 100000 -c 250 (one run of about 1 s per proxy) through prebuilt Docker images on an i5-13600K PC, with each proxy and the echo backend capped at 4 CPUs. Spire got 114,512 req/s vs HAProxy 2.7.3 85,406 and Envoy 1.22.8 48,040, but the load generator had 12 CPUs only in the Spire and nginx runs; tuned nginx 1.23.3 reached 148,677 (Spire 0.77x), and with equal load-generator CPUs in 2023 Spire was 0.81x HAProxy. A third-party run (holmofy/proxy-benchmark, Sept 2024, i7-13700H laptop, wrk -t4 -c1000 -d120s from the host) put Silverwind 0.0.20 at 19,352 req/s vs HAProxy 17,826 (1.09x) and Envoy 13,517 (1.43x), but Silverwind's backend was lsk569937453/echo-server:0.0.3 (about 80 bytes per response) while the others used jmalloc/echo-server (169-335 bytes), and that run's nginx row returned 29,520 non-2xx responses.
status_note: Active but quiet (last commit and crates.io release 0.0.28 on 2026-01-28), Apache-2.0 (license file named 'licence'), single-maintainer pre-1.0 gateway that is usable as a binary; its speed claim over C and C++ proxies rests on a harness that gave the load generator 12 CPUs only for Spire and nginx and probably left HAProxy and Envoy oversubscribed inside a 4-CPU quota, so treat it as a feature-rich gateway, not a faster one.
